items.title: The sum of all positive integers equals minus one twelfth
items.claim: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... = -1/12. This obviously fails as a normal sum (it diverges to infinity). But it is the value of the Riemann zeta function analytically continued to s = -1, and it shows up in physics (Casimir effect, string theory).
items.prompt: How does an obviously divergent sum get a finite value?

options.text: Analytic continuation extends a function defined on one domain (where the series converges) to a larger domain (where the series doesn't); zeta(-1) is well-defined as a function value even though the corresponding series diverges
Negative numbers were added without permission

items.reveal_title: Ramanujan, Hardy, and the strange identity
items.reveal:
Srinivasa Ramanujan wrote to Hardy in 1913 claiming results like 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... = -1/12. Hardy initially thought Ramanujan must be a crank — until he checked.

The Riemann zeta function is defined by zeta(s) = sum from n=1 to infinity of 1/n to the power s, but only when the real part of s exceeds 1. The function extends analytically to the whole complex plane (except a pole at s = 1). At s = -1, zeta(-1) = -1/12.

If you formally substitute s = -1 into the series, you get 1 + 2 + 3 + ... The series doesn't converge there — but the function it defined still has a value, just by a different (analytic continuation) method.

In quantum field theory, the same -1/12 appears. The Casimir force calculation involves summing zero-point energies of standing waves; this sum diverges, but the physical answer obtained by zeta regularisation matches experiment.

The identity is not casually 'true' as arithmetic. It's true as the value of a specific extension of the zeta function — and that extension happens to give physically correct predictions.
items.why: Treating divergent sums as if they have finite values seems like a trick — but in the right framework, analytic continuation gives them precise meanings that physics turns out to use.

items.title: Tilting your phone changes things differently depending on the order
items.claim: Take a book. Rotate 90 degrees about its vertical axis, then 90 degrees about its horizontal axis. Now reset and reverse the order: horizontal first, then vertical. The book ends up in a DIFFERENT orientation. Rotations in 3D do not commute.

options.text: Rotation matrices in 3D are non-commutative — R1 * R2 is not equal to R2 * R1 in general. SO(3) is a non-abelian Lie group, unlike rotations in 2D which DO commute

items.reveal:
Rotations in 2D (the plane): R(theta1) * R(theta2) = R(theta1 + theta2) = R(theta2) * R(theta1). They commute. The group SO(2) is abelian.

Rotations in 3D: not commutative. The group SO(3) is non-abelian. The order in which you apply rotations changes the final orientation.

Experiment: rotate book 90° about vertical (y-axis) — left becomes back. Then rotate 90° about (now front-pointing) x-axis — back becomes bottom. Reset. Now rotate 90° about x first — top becomes back. Then 90° about y — back becomes left. Final orientations differ.

Mathematically: if R_x is rotation about x-axis and R_y about y-axis, R_x R_y is not equal to R_y R_x. The 'commutator' [R_x, R_y] = R_x R_y - R_y R_x is non-zero, representing a small rotation about the third axis.

Consequences:
- Aerospace: gimbal lock — a 3-axis gyroscope can have its three rotation axes align such that one rotational degree of freedom is lost. Famously almost killed Apollo astronauts on Apollo 11.
- Quaternions (Hamilton 1843) parametrise 3D rotations without gimbal lock and are standard in 3D graphics.
- Quantum mechanics: angular momentum operators have the same commutation structure as 3D rotations, leading to quantisation.

In higher dimensions (n > 3), rotation groups SO(n) are also non-commutative.
items.why: Rotation seems like a simple geometric concept. In 3D it's surprisingly subtle — the order matters, and that fact has cost lives, structured quantum mechanics, and shaped every video game engine.
